artifact.description: A list of the points where the workflow could continue on language alone, with the evidence that must be fetched at each one, the filter applied before anything reaches the model, the check that fires, and what happens when it does, alongside source-contract.md holding the scope, citation rule, refusal path and assumption rule for the deliverable.

verification: Every guessing point names the specific evidence that has to be read before an answer can be produced.
Privacy and scope filters are applied when the material is assembled, not requested in the instructions.
Each consequential claim carries its source beside the sentence rather than in an appendix.
The plan states separately what a provenance check proves and what it does not prove.
You removed a supporting document, reran, and recorded whether the workflow refused or invented.

content.text: Ask what happens when it is tempted to guess

There is one question that sorts loose setups from sound ones. When the system does not have what it needs, can it keep going anyway on fluent language alone? If it can, the setup is too loose. If it has to fetch the evidence, confirm the evidence is current, and build the answer out of what came back, then it will still fail sometimes, but it will fail with a gap, a caveat or an empty result rather than a confident invention.

This matters more than it sounds. An answer that reads well and cites the wrong number is worse than a slow manual process, because the slow process is at least honest about what it can do. An obviously incomplete spreadsheet gets questioned. A paragraph that sounds finished often does not.
So walk your workflow and mark the guessing points: every step where the output could be produced without a specific input having actually been read. Those marks are the whole of this lesson's work.
Filter before the model, not with it
Do not ask a model to apply your constraints while it answers. Apply them to what you hand over.

Privacy comes first. Whatever must not be seen should not be in the material you supply, which means redaction, entitlement rules and access limits belong at the point where the pack is assembled. A rule enforced in the wording of a request is a request. A rule enforced by not including the material is a boundary.

Scope works the same way. If only this quarter's records are relevant, hand over this quarter's records. Asking a system to consider only recent material while giving it everything is a reliable way to get a confident claim about something from two years ago, described as recent, with a source that genuinely exists.

This is the cheap exact work from the last section applied to the input. Selecting the right material is quick, repeatable, and checkable by somebody who never reads the output. Doing that selection with a model is none of those things.
Put the source next to the claim

For consequential claims, the source belongs beside the sentence it supports. A list of references at the end helps somebody navigate, but it does not establish which source belongs to which claim, and a reviewer cannot check it in the time they actually have.

The rule is short: no source, no claim. Saying there is not enough evidence has to be permitted. Inventing evidence does not. And where you can check anything mechanically, check that every source cited is one of the documents you actually supplied. Anything cited from outside that set was invented, however plausible the reference looks.
Provenance is not support
These are two separate tests and running them together is where people get hurt.

Provenance asks whether the cited source exists in the material that was provided. It is cheap, it can be automated, and it is usually all a check gives you. Support asks whether that source actually justifies the claim, which is a different question needing a bounded evaluation, a rule where one exists, or a person for anything high risk.

A citation proves the source was available. It does not prove the source says what the sentence says. Write that limit down next to your check, in the check's own words, because the next person to read it will assume it covers more than it does. That assumption is how a validated-looking document gets acted on.
Keep the not enough evidence path open

Forcing an answer guarantees invention whenever the answer is not in the material. So refusal has to be a real outcome with somewhere honest to go: show the retrieved material without the synthesis, escalate to the person who can decide, or mark the section as unresolved and carry on with the rest.

Treat assumptions as evidence too. Where a claim rests on an assumption rather than a source, name the assumption, name what it is sensitive to, and name the limit of the estimate. A hidden assumption is what makes a number unreviewable, and an unreviewable number in a document that looks rigorous is the worst combination available.
Illustrative source contract: a quarterly supplier review

This contract is invented for teaching. The supplier, the pack and the rules are constructed to show the shape of a working source contract. It is not a real policy and it should not be copied into live use without your own legal and procurement input.
The deliverable is a quarterly supplier review note that ends in a renewal recommendation. The contract covers six things.
Scope of material. The four supplier files for this quarter and the signed agreement. Nothing outside that set may be cited, and nothing outside it is supplied.
Filters applied at assembly. Records dated inside the quarter only. Commercial terms removed for anyone outside procurement. Third-party references removed under the confidentiality clause.
Citation form. Each claim ends with the document name and the section or row it came from, in the sentence, not in a footnote.
Claims that may not appear without a source. Anything about spend, delivery performance, contractual obligation, or renewal terms.
Refusal path. Where the pack does not settle a question, the note says not enough evidence and names what would settle it.
Assumption rule. Any figure projected forwards states its base, the assumption applied, and the range it is sensitive to.

The contract also states its own limit, which is the part that makes it honest. Every claim gets a provenance check, meaning somebody confirms the cited document is in the pack. Only the three claims that drive the renewal recommendation get a support check, where a reviewer opens the cited section and confirms it says what the sentence says. Everything else carries provenance only, and the note says so, so that nobody mistakes a full reference list for a fully verified document.
What you will make
guardrail-plan.md, listing each guessing point with the evidence that must be fetched and the check that fires.
For each check, what happens when it fires: refuse, clarify, escalate, or continue with the section marked.
source-contract.md, with scope, filters, citation form, protected claims, refusal path and assumption rule.
A written statement of which claims get a support check and which get provenance only.
Try it on your work
Take a finished output from your job and pick three factual sentences. For each, try to find the exact source. Note how long it took.
Walk the workflow and mark every step that could produce an answer without a specific input having been read.
For each mark, write what has to be fetched first and what the step does when the fetch comes back empty.
Move every privacy and scope rule out of your instructions and into how the material is assembled. Write down what you moved.
Write the source contract for the deliverable, including which claims require a source and which get a support check.
Remove one supporting document from the pack and run the job again. Watch whether the output refuses, marks the gap, or writes smoothly around it.
Record what happened. Writing round the gap is the result that needs the repair, and it is also the most common one.
Check your work
Every guessing point names specific evidence, not a general instruction to be careful.
No privacy or scope rule survives only as wording in a request.
A reviewer can check any consequential claim without leaving the sentence it sits in.
The plan says in plain words what a provenance check proves and what it leaves open.
The refusal path has a destination, not just permission to refuse.
The document-removal test was actually run and its result is recorded, including the uncomfortable version.
If the run with the missing document produced an answer that read perfectly well, you have found the most valuable thing in this lesson. That is the failure your recipients would never have noticed.

lessons.title: Leave a replayable decision trace
lessons.outcome: Record one consequential decision so somebody else can replay it: rule version, sourced facts, gaps, intermediate results, assumptions, outcome and required action, plus a short map telling them where to start.
lessons.exercise: Take one consequential decision from your job and record it as a trace covering the version of the rule you applied, every fact with its source, the facts that were missing or in conflict, the intermediate results, the assumptions, the outcome and the action it requires. Then write a review map of no more than five bullets, hand both to a colleague, and ask them to reach the same outcome from the record alone.

artifact.description: A record of one consequential decision holding the dated rule version, every fact with its source, the missing conflicting or superseded facts, each intermediate result, the assumptions named as assumptions, the outcome and required action, accompanied by review-map.md and the notes from a colleague who tried to replay it.

verification: The rule version is recorded with a date, so a later reader knows which version produced this outcome.
Every fact carries the source it came from, and gaps are listed rather than omitted.
The intermediate results show which conditions actually determined the outcome.
The trace states plainly what it does not prove about the rule or the interpretation.
A colleague replayed it from the record and their questions are written down.

content.text: The record is the explanation

When a decision follows a rule, the explanation people actually need is the replayable record of how it was reached, not a paragraph describing what the system was thinking. Prose can summarise that record and often should. But if the prose and the record disagree, the record wins, and everybody should know that in advance.

This is also how you stop chasing hidden reasoning. Asking a model to explain itself produces something readable and unstable, and it is not an audit record. A reviewer does not need to know what was going on inside anything. They need the rule, the evidence that was accepted, and the working that connected them.
What goes in the trace
The exact version of the rule that was applied, with a date. Not the rule as it stands today, the one in force at the time.
Every fact that was used, with the source it came from.
Facts that were missing, in conflict, superseded, or that could not be retrieved. This is the part people leave out and the part reviewers need most.
Each intermediate result: which conditions were met, which thresholds were crossed, which gates passed.
Which of those actually determined the outcome, as distinct from which merely ran.
The assumptions, labelled as assumptions, with what each one is sensitive to.
The outcome and the action it requires of somebody.
The following sketch is invented for teaching and does not describe any real case.

A short worked shape, continuing the supplier review. Rule version: renewal guidance version four, dated the first of the quarter. Facts: delivery performance from the quarterly file, section three; spend against agreement from the finance export, row twelve; one open dispute from the contract log. Gaps: the satisfaction survey was not returned this quarter, so that input is missing rather than zero. Intermediate results: performance threshold met, spend within tolerance, dispute gate not cleared. Determining node: the dispute gate. Assumptions: the dispute resolves within the standard window, sensitive to the counterparty's response time. Outcome: renew with a conditional clause. Required action: procurement lead to confirm the dispute position before signature.
Notice how much of that is unremarkable. That is the point. A useful trace is boring to read and quick to argue with, which is exactly what you want when somebody disagrees.
The review map
The trace tells a reviewer everything. The map tells them where to start, which is a different job and takes about a minute to write.

Keep it to two or three bullets for something small and five at most for anything larger. Begin with the core decision, then name what supports it, then point at what proves it, then call out the risky edge or the place where judgement was genuinely required. Do not write a second summary underneath it. If the map needs ten bullets, the work needs reshaping rather than a longer map.

The same shape serves two people. As the author, the map is part of what you hand over: it helps somebody else enter work whose thinking they did not watch unfold, which matters more when a system produced the first draft. As the reviewer, writing your own map before commenting forces you to say what the work is really about, and it stops you producing reasonable-sounding remarks that are not tied to the decision or the risk.
What the trace does not prove
A trace proves one thing: that the recorded facts propagated through a specific rule to produce this outcome. That is genuinely useful and it is also all it proves.

It does not prove the rule was a good rule. It does not prove each fact was interpreted correctly. A complete, tidy, fully populated record can sit underneath a decision that was wrong for either reason, and its tidiness will make the decision harder to challenge rather than easier.

Keeping the three failures separate is what makes them repairable. A bad fact needs a better source or a better interpretation check. A bad rule needs the people who own the rule to change it. A bad propagation needs the mechanism fixed. When somebody says the system got this wrong, the first useful question is which of the three they mean, and the trace is what lets them answer.

Write that limit into the trace itself, in a line of its own. Otherwise a reader treats a complete-looking record as proof of correctness, which is the failure this whole practice was meant to prevent.
What you will make
decision-trace.md for one consequential decision, covering all seven parts above.
A stated limit line saying what the trace proves and what it leaves open.
review-map.md, five bullets at most, telling a reader where to start.
The replay notes from the colleague who tried to reach your outcome from the record alone.
Try it on your work
Choose one decision from the last month that somebody could reasonably challenge. Avoid the easy ones.
Write down the rule you applied and give it a version and a date, even if you are inventing the numbering today.
List every fact with its source. Where you cannot find the source, say so rather than dropping the fact.
List what was missing, stale or contradictory at the time. Resist tidying this section.
Record the intermediate results and mark which one actually decided the outcome.
Separate the assumptions from the facts and say what each assumption is sensitive to.
Write the map, hand both to a colleague, and ask them to reach the outcome without talking to you. Write down every question they had to ask anyway.
Check your work
The rule version is dated, so a reader can tell which version was in force.
Every fact has a source, and missing facts appear as missing rather than as zero or absent.
The determining condition is marked, so a reader knows which part to argue with.
Assumptions are labelled as assumptions and carry what they are sensitive to.
The limit line is present and says what the trace does not establish.
The map is five bullets or fewer and does not repeat itself as a summary.
The colleague's questions are recorded verbatim, including the ones that make the record look bad.
Every question your colleague had to ask is a hole in the trace. Fix the trace rather than answering the question, because the next reader will not have you sitting beside them.

technicalExtension.title: Optional lab: validate citations, replay policy, and shadow a version change
technicalExtension.outcome: Enforce structured citations against the retrieved candidate set, keep policy pure enough that replay is free, and compare two policy versions on the same facts before either one enforces anything.

content.text: Why this is optional
The core lessons taught source adjacency and the trace as judgement you apply by hand. This lab is the enforceable version for people building the system. Nothing in the next section depends on it.
Both halves or neither

The contract has two halves and each is useless alone. The request requires structured citations: strict output shape, every claim carrying evidence identifiers, no claim without one, and an explicit path for declaring there is not enough evidence. The validator then walks every cited identifier and checks it against the candidate set you actually retrieved and supplied. Asking politely for citations without validating them gets you fabricated identifiers in exactly the right shape. Validating without requiring them leaves nothing to validate.

When the validator rejects, the feature needs somewhere honest to go, usually showing the retrieved material with no synthesis at all. Rejecting into a silent fallback that answers anyway rebuilds the problem you just solved. And note the residual next to the check in the code: membership proves the source was in the allowed set, never that the span supports the claim.
Purity is what makes replay free

Keep the policy evaluation pure: no clock read, no database call, no model call inside it. Facts go in, a decision and a trace come out. Once that holds, replay is not a feature you build, it is a property you already have, and the trace can generate counterfactuals without another reasoning prompt by asking which smallest fact change would flip the outcome.

Record each decision the way policy-engine tooling does: a decision identifier, the input the policy was given, and the metadata of the exact policy bundle that ran. That triple is what makes a decision auditable months later, when the current version of the rule has moved on and the question is what was in force at the time.
Shadow the version change

Before a new policy version enforces anything, run it beside the current one on the same facts and record only the disagreements. That gives you the real divergence rate rather than the one your fixtures suggested, and it gives promotion a trigger you can point at. Where the two versions differ, the trace shows which node produced the difference, which turns an argument about whether the update is safe into a list of specific cases to review.

sections.title: Close delegated work properly
sections.outcome: Carry delegated work through to an actual closing state rather than stopping at the moment somebody says it is finished, and write the contract that says what may be touched and what happens when the automation fails.

lessons.title: Treat done as a claim
lessons.outcome: Keep a ledger that carries every delegated piece of work through claimed, reviewed, accepted or rejected, superseded, integrated and cleaned, and capture what each piece taught you.
lessons.exercise: Delegate a bounded batch of at least three pieces of work, to colleagues, to a tool, or to both. Open the ledger before you delegate rather than afterwards, and carry each item through the states, recording the review evidence, the reason for anything rejected or superseded, where the work actually ended up, and what each item taught you that the next delegation should know.

artifact.description: A ledger covering a real batch of delegated work, with one row per item holding the task, who or what did it, where the artefact lives, the current claim state, the review evidence, the integration state, the cleanup state, the reason for anything that did not ship, and what the item taught you.

verification: Every item has a closing state, and rejected or superseded counts as closed with a recorded reason.
Each accepted item names the evidence that somebody actually reviewed it against the requirement.
Integration state says where the work now lives, not merely that it was finished.
Cleanup state is recorded, including anything deliberately kept and why it was kept.
At least one learning is written down and carried into how you delegated the next item.
sourceNotes: Parallel Agent Work Needs a Closing Ledger.md

content.text: A stopped worker is not a delivered result

Three different things get called done and only one of them is. The work stopped. The artefact exists. The result is in the hands of the person who needed it and they have accepted it. Most of the trouble in delegated work comes from treating the first as though it were the third.

When you delegate to a colleague, the gap is usually visible. You notice the note never arrived. When you delegate to a tool, the gap hides, because the session ends with something that reads like completion. The conversation finished, the summary sounded confident, and it is genuinely hard to remember that nothing has happened yet.

So treat done as a claim. It still has to pass review, acceptance, arrival in the place the work actually lives, and cleanup. Every one of those is a separate event, and any of them can quietly fail to happen.
The states worth tracking
Claimed. Somebody or something has said the work is finished. This is where most tracking stops and where real tracking starts.
Reviewed. A person has looked at it against the requirement, and there is evidence that the looking happened rather than a memory of intending to.
Accepted. Whoever owns the outcome agrees it meets the requirement.
Rejected. It does not meet the requirement, and the reason is written down. This is a perfectly good closing state.
Superseded. Something else has replaced it. Also a good closing state, and the one people forget, which is why old versions sit around looking current.
Integrated. It is in the place the work actually lives, rather than in a draft, a chat thread, or somebody's downloads folder.
Cleaned. The working material is put away, or deliberately kept with a stated reason. Drafts closed, spare copies removed, threads archived.

That list reads like administration and it protects judgement. Without it you will eventually confuse the worker stopped talking with the work shipped, or this was approved with this can be forgotten. Both mistakes are quiet and both are expensive.
The ledger and the map do different jobs

The review map from the last lesson helps one person enter one artefact: where to start, what supports it, what proves it, where the judgement sits. The ledger closes a whole batch. They are not competing and neither replaces the other.

If you delegate one thing at a time, your ledger is three lines and it is still worth keeping, because the habit is what survives. The failure it prevents scales with how many things are in flight, and the number in flight has a way of growing without anybody deciding it should.
Carry the learnings forward

Whoever coordinates the work holds context that no individual worker has. A colleague who discovered the source data was wrong, or a tool session that found the template had changed last month, learned something the next piece of work needs and will otherwise never receive.

So the ledger carries one more column: what this item taught us. Read that column before the next delegation. Anything in it that has now appeared twice belongs in your rules file rather than in the ledger, because a learning that recurs is a rule you have not written down yet.
The honest reason to stay in some loops
Running work end to end without touching it is possible for plenty of tasks, and the reasons to stay involved are usually not about capability.

The first is trust. There is always a variable. When it gets something wrong, that is yours, because your name is on the result and nobody downstream will care who drafted it. The second is learning. When it runs entirely without you, you do not build the understanding, and you often spend the saved time reading through what it did anyway to work out whether you agree.

A reasonable position: hand over the whole thing for simple, low-stakes work, and stay in the loop for anything you actually care about, while still letting the delegation do the gathering, the research and the first draft. That is a risk choice made deliberately, task by task, and the ledger is where you record which choice you made.
What you will make
closing-ledger.md, one row per delegated item in a real batch of at least three.
Columns for task, who or what did it, where the artefact lives, claim state, review evidence, integration state and cleanup state.
A reason recorded against everything that did not ship.
A learnings column, and a note on which learnings you promoted into your rules.
Try it on your work
Pick a bounded batch of at least three pieces of work you would delegate anyway. Colleagues, a tool, or a mix.
Open the ledger before you delegate anything. A ledger written afterwards is a memoir.
As each item comes back, record the claim, then stop. Do not mark anything accepted in the same movement.
Review each item against the requirement from your baseline and record what you checked, not merely that you checked.
Move each item to accepted, rejected or superseded. Force yourself to close every row; an item with no closing state is the thing this lesson exists to catch.
Record where each accepted item actually ended up, then do the cleanup and record that too.
Read the learnings column before your next delegation and change one thing about how you brief it.
Check your work
No row is left sitting at claimed. Every item reached a closing state.
Review evidence names what was checked, so somebody else could tell whether the review had teeth.
Rejected and superseded items carry reasons a reader could act on.
Integration state says where the work lives now, and you could open it from that description.
Anything deliberately left uncleaned has a stated reason rather than being forgotten.
At least one learning changed how you briefed the next item, and the ledger says which.

lessons.title: Design for automation failure
lessons.outcome: Write a delegation contract with an explicit blast radius, preflight, readiness signal, side-effect boundary, snapshot and recovery step, then test one likely timing failure without using sensitive live input.
lessons.exercise: Rewrite the instruction you use to delegate your job so that it states what may be touched and what may not, what is checked before anything changes, what signal proves the target is ready, what is captured first, and how the change would be undone. Then pick the failure you think is most likely, design a harmless observation that would distinguish it from at least two other causes, and run that observation using invented or copied input rather than anything live.

artifact.description: A delegation instruction stating the blast radius, the preflight checks, the readiness signal, the side-effect boundary, the snapshot and what restoring it involves, the mutation itself, and the tested recovery step, alongside automation-failure-runbook.md listing the three most likely failures, the observation that tells them apart, and the recovery for each.

verification: The contract names what may be touched and states plainly that everything else is out of bounds.
The readiness signal is something observable rather than an assumption that the target looks ready.
The snapshot names what it captures and what restoring it would actually involve.
The recovery step was run at least once against a copy, and the result is recorded.
The runbook lists at least three candidate causes and the observation that distinguishes them.
sourceNotes: Front-Load the Checks That Can Fail.md

content.text: Say what may be touched
Before delegating anything that changes something, write down what the work is allowed to touch. Everything else is out of bounds, and saying so explicitly costs you one sentence.

Touch only what the task requires. Do not tidy adjacent things that look untidy. Do not remove things that appear unused. Do not add improvements nobody asked for. Where something adjacent genuinely looks wrong, report it at the end as an observation and let a person decide, rather than acting on it in passing.

This matters more with automation than with a colleague. A person hesitates before doing something large that nobody asked for. Automation does not hesitate, and a helpful tidy-up performed across the wrong scope is one of the more unpleasant ways to spend an afternoon.
The six parts of the contract
Preflight. Everything you can verify without changing anything: the inputs exist, the approvals are in place, the target is the thing you believe it is.
Readiness signal. Something you can observe that proves the target is ready to be acted on. Not that it looks ready, and not that it usually is by now.
Side-effect boundary. The explicit list of what may be changed, sent or created. Anything outside the list is a stop and a question, not a judgement call.
Snapshot. What you capture so you can get back, and what restoring it actually involves in steps somebody else could follow.
Mutation. The change itself, kept as small as it can be while still doing the job.
Recovery. The step that undoes or repairs it, written before the mutation runs and tested at least once against a copy.
The ordering is the same principle as the last section. The parts that can fail cheaply run first, and the part that cannot be undone runs last, behind all of them.
Automation falls into gaps people never notice

Interactive things are built for human speed. A person sees a prompt, pauses for half a second, then types. Automation answers instantly, and it can land its answer before the thing on the other side has finished getting ready to receive it. The prompt appearing and the program being ready to read are two separate events, and only automation is quick enough to fall between them.

The same shape turns up everywhere once you know to look for it. Pressing a button before the thing behind it is connected. Sending a request to a service that is accepting connections but has not finished loading. Typing into a session that is still starting up. Every layer has a gap between looking ready and being ready, and automation finds all of them.
The rule that follows is short. When automation fails in a way a manual run does not, suspect timing before content.
Diagnose without blaming the input

The trap is specific and it catches careful people. Correct input goes in, the system rejects it, and you go hunting for wrong-input causes. You retype the value, you check it character by character, you assume the record is stale, and you burn attempts on something that was never wrong.

Prove the timing harmlessly instead. Do not submit the real thing again. Send something inert at the moment the step appears to be ready and observe whether the system behaves as though it were listening. If it does not, you have your answer without having submitted anything sensitive and without risking a lockout or a duplicate record. A diagnostic that cannot cause damage is worth more than a clever theory.

The non-technical version is the same move. Before assuming the data was wrong, check whether the step ran at the moment you think it ran, and whether it read the version of the file you think it read. Make the cheapest observation that would tell the candidate causes apart.

Three habits keep this honest. Do not take the first explanation that fits: write down at least three possible causes and say which observation would separate them, then go and make that observation. State the problem in plain language before you fix anything, because a problem you cannot state plainly is a problem you have not found. And when you do fix it, change as little as you can, so that the next failure tells you something rather than arriving inside a pile of unrelated edits.
What you will make
delegation-contract.md, covering blast radius, preflight, readiness signal, side-effect boundary, snapshot, mutation and recovery.
automation-failure-runbook.md, listing the three failures you think most likely.
For each failure, the observation that would distinguish it from the others, and the recovery.
A record of the one timing test you ran, including what you sent and what you saw.
Try it on your work
Take the instruction you currently use to delegate your job and read it as though you were the one receiving it. Note everything it leaves to inference.
Write the blast radius as two lists: may touch, and must not touch. Be specific enough that a stranger could apply it.
Name the readiness signal. If your answer is that it is usually fine by then, you have found a gap rather than a signal.
Write the snapshot and then actually restore from it once, on a copy, to see whether the steps you wrote are the steps it takes.
List three plausible causes for the failure you most expect, and design one harmless observation that separates them.
Run that observation using invented or copied input. Nothing live, nothing sensitive, no real recipients.
Write the runbook from what you learnt, and record the case where the observation told you nothing, if that is what happened.
Check your work
The contract states what is out of bounds, not only what is in scope.
The readiness signal is observable, and you could say how you would observe it.
The snapshot has been restored from at least once rather than merely described.
The recovery step existed before the mutation step was written.
The runbook names three causes, so the first plausible one was not simply accepted.
The diagnostic you ran could not have caused damage, and the record says why not.
Nothing live, sensitive or recipient-facing was involved in the test.

If you could not think of three causes, that usually means you have already decided what the answer is. Write the two you dismissed and say what evidence dismissed them, because that is the part you will want when the failure returns looking slightly different.

technicalExtension.title: Optional lab: run the ledger across branches, worktrees and threads
technicalExtension.outcome: Apply the closing ledger to parallel agent delivery so that branches, worktrees, test claims, rebases, merges and archived threads all reach a recorded state instead of becoming folklore.
sourceNotes: Parallel Agent Work Needs a Closing Ledger.md

content.text: Why this is optional

The core lesson taught the ledger for any kind of delegation. This lab is the version for running several coding agents at once, where the leftover state is version control rather than drafts. Nothing in the final section depends on it.
The extra columns

Splitting work across many agent threads only helps if the orchestrator keeps a real closing ledger. For each worker, track the task, the branch, the worktree path, the current claim of running, blocked, ready for review, superseded, merged or rejected, the review evidence of diff read and tests checked and risk noted, the integration state of rebased, merged, conflicted or deliberately left out, and the cleanup state of thread archived and worktree removed or preserved with a reason.

# what is actually in flight
git worktree list
git branch --list 'agent/*' --format='%(refname:short) %(upstream:track)'

# what the claim is worth
git log --oneline main..agent/topic
git diff --stat main...agent/topic

# cleanup only once integration state is recorded
git worktree remove ../wt-agent-topic
git branch -d agent/topic
The two failures this catches

The first is a branch superseded by a safer fix made on a different branch. The code is fine and the workflow memory is not: without a recorded superseded state, the abandoned branch keeps looking like pending work, and somebody eventually reviews or revives it. The second is threads left open after their work has already merged or been deliberately closed. Nothing is broken, but the set of open threads stops meaning anything, which is the same as having no signal at all.

Parallel agents manufacture state: branches, worktrees, review summaries, test claims and thread status. That is another generated surface, and like every generated surface it needs a source of truth and a moment where it is reconciled. Without one it becomes stale context wearing a better label. The rule of thumb is that no cleanup command runs until the integration state for that row has been written down, because once the branch is gone the evidence of what happened to it is gone too.

sections.title: Choose the work surface
sections.outcome: Choose between a quick conversation and delegated multi-step work from the shape and risk of the job, then record what the current product surface can and cannot establish.

lessons.title: Separate chat from delegated work
lessons.outcome: Classify your recurring job as a quick conversation or a bounded delegation, and define the scope, inputs, authority, progress signals and finish condition before work starts.
lessons.exercise: Take the recurring job from your baseline, split its requests into quick questions and delegated work, then write a work-surface decision that names the inputs, authority boundary, progress checkpoints, finish condition and recovery path for the next real run.

artifact.description: A decision record classifying the chosen job as chat, delegated work or a deliberate sequence of both, with its scope, inputs, allowed actions, progress signals, finish condition, review owner and recovery path.

verification: Each request is classified from the work it requires rather than from which product button is easiest to reach.
The delegated part has a written finish condition that another person could inspect without reading the conversation.
The authority boundary names an action the system must stop before taking, even if it appears to know what should happen.
At least one progress checkpoint can expose a wrong direction before the final artefact is produced.
The record says who adopts the result and remains responsible for checking it before use.

content.text: Choose from the job, not the button

A chat surface is useful when you need a quick explanation, a question answered, a small draft or help thinking through one decision. You stay in the conversation, inspect each response and decide the next move. The work is short enough that you can hold its state and notice when it has wandered.

A delegated work surface is for a bounded job with several steps, source material, an artefact to produce and a finish condition. The system may plan the route, ask questions, work across files and report progress. That does not make the job unowned. Delegation changes who performs steps. It does not transfer the responsibility for adopting the result.

The distinction is about the shape of the work, not about which product looks newer. A short question can sit inside a delegated job. A long conversation can still be chat if you are choosing every next step yourself. Write down who controls scope, sequence and action. That tells you which surface you are actually using.
Six fields make a delegation bounded
Scope names the one job and what remains outside it. A request to prepare a review pack does not silently include sending it.
Inputs name the approved sources and the date or version that matters. Missing material becomes a question or a refusal, not an invitation to fill the gap.
Authority says what may be read, drafted and changed. It also says which external action needs a person to approve it.
Progress signals show the plan, sources found, open questions and draft state early enough for you to redirect the job.
Finish states the required artefact and the checks it must pass. A response that says complete is not a finish condition.
Recovery says what happens if the work stops, uses the wrong source or reaches an action it cannot safely take.

If you cannot fill these fields, keep the work conversational while you find the missing policy or evidence. A delegated surface cannot repair an undefined job. It can only move through the ambiguity with more freedom, which is precisely when the boundary matters.
Split a job without splitting ownership

Many useful workflows use both surfaces. You might use chat to challenge the purpose of a report, then delegate evidence gathering and a first draft, then return to chat to test an assumption. The decision is made step by step. There is no prize for making the whole job autonomous.

For each step, ask who chooses the next move and whether the step can change something outside the working draft. If you choose the next move, it is conversational. If the system chooses several moves inside a bounded contract, it is delegated. If it can send, publish, update or delete, you also need an explicit action gate.

The evidence of a good choice is not that the run felt impressive. It is that the surface matched the job, missing information became visible, review happened before adoption, and the result reached the finish condition without crossing the authority boundary.
What you will make

Create work-surface-decision.md. Record the job, each major step, whether that step is chat or delegated work, the reason, the six boundary fields, and the person who accepts the final result. Keep product names out of the first pass so the job drives the decision.
Try it on your work
Open your real-task baseline and list the decisions and artefacts the job contains.
Mark each step chat, delegated work or person-only. Give one sentence of evidence for the mark.
Complete the scope, inputs, authority, progress, finish and recovery fields for every delegated step.
Ask a colleague to find the point where the system could do more than you intended. Tighten that boundary before the run.
Run one low-risk instance and record where you had to redirect, approve or take the work back.
Check your work
A reader can tell why each step needs conversation, delegation or a person.
No delegated step has an open-ended scope or an unnamed input source.
At least one checkpoint would catch a plausible wrong direction before the finished artefact.
Every external action has a named approval point and a named approver.
The run record names what the system did and what you remained responsible for.

lessons.title: Map current work surfaces
lessons.outcome: Build a dated map of the work surfaces available to you, distinguish their documented roles, and test access on your actual account without turning capability into a performance claim.
lessons.exercise: Inspect the products approved for your work, record which named surfaces your account actually exposes, map each surface to one step in your recurring job, and mark every capability that still needs a live test or administrator decision.

artifact.description: A dated product map recording the documented role, actual account access, permitted data, permitted actions, live test result and review trigger for each work surface considered for the recurring job.

verification: The map is labelled As of 14 August 2026 and gives every product observation a review trigger.
ChatGPT Work and Codex are recorded as different surfaces with different documented centres of work.
Claude Cowork and Copilot Cowork are not treated as the same product despite the shared word Cowork.
Every capability is marked documented, observed on this account, unavailable, or not yet tested.
No entry turns a vendor capability statement into evidence of speed, accuracy, quality or suitability.

content.text: A dated field map

As of 14 August 2026, the main products in this lesson separate quick conversation from longer delegated work in different ways. The names, plans, interfaces and permissions can change. Treat this as a field map for one date, then inspect the account and organisation you actually use.

A product page can establish a documented capability. It cannot establish that the capability performs your job well. Current capability is not performance evidence. Your dated-product-map.md keeps documented, observed and approved as separate columns so those claims cannot collapse into one another.
OpenAI surfaces

ChatGPT Work is the current OpenAI surface for longer, multi-step professional work and finished deliverables such as research, documents, spreadsheets, presentations and reports. A user can inspect progress, answer questions, redirect the work and approve important actions. Availability and file behaviour still depend on the plan, platform, connected apps and workspace controls.

Codex is the dedicated OpenAI surface for software development and technical work, including code, commands, tests and repositories. It can be useful to a technical practitioner working with files or data, but it is not the default non-technical work surface in this course. ChatGPT Work versus Codex is a job distinction, not a contest.
Anthropic and Microsoft surfaces

Claude Cowork is Anthropic's multi-step knowledge-work surface. Its documentation covers research, files, documents, spreadsheets, presentations, projects, scheduled work and delegated tasks. Local files, browser control, remote work and live artefacts vary by platform and mode, so record what you can actually see rather than copying the full feature list.

Microsoft 365 Copilot is the Microsoft work surface connected to applications such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams and, where licensed and configured, organisational work data. Copilot Chat, Researcher, Analyst and file agents have distinct roles. Access depends on licence, tenant configuration and administrator settings.

Copilot Cowork is Microsoft's delegated work experience inside Microsoft 365 Copilot. It can carry multi-step work across Microsoft 365, including documents, messages, meetings and files, with action approvals. It is not Claude Cowork. Microsoft uses Anthropic technology within a separate Microsoft product, identity and governance boundary.
Use four evidence states
Documented means the vendor currently describes the capability. It does not mean your plan includes it.
Observed means you opened your account and verified the surface, control or result yourself on the date recorded.
Approved means your organisation permits the data and action involved. Product access is not organisational approval.
Suitable means the surface passed your job-specific check. It is the conclusion of a test, not a fact borrowed from documentation.

If any state is missing, record it. Do not smooth not tested into supported, and do not smooth supported into safe. The gap tells you whether the next step is a harmless live test, a policy question, an administrator request or a decision to use invented input.
What you will make

Create dated-product-map.md. Give each surface a row for documented role, plan or platform caveat, actual access, approved data class, permitted action, evidence from one low-risk test and the event or date that should trigger a review.
Try it on your work
List only products your organisation approves or that you can test with invented material.
Open each account and record the named surfaces you can reach. Mark anything absent rather than guessing why.
Choose one harmless step from your recurring job and run the same source pack and acceptance check on each suitable surface.
Record the actual questions, actions and output. Keep this evidence separate from the vendor's description.
Choose a surface for this job and write the dated reason. Add the condition that would make you review the choice.
Check your work
Every current product fact carries the date and is traceable through the source map.
The map distinguishes product documentation, account observation, organisational approval and job suitability.
ChatGPT Work, Codex, Claude Cowork, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Cowork each have a separate row.
No missing feature, licence or permission has been silently treated as present.
The chosen surface passed a requirement-derived check on your job rather than a prose-quality preference.

sections.title: Package repeated work
sections.outcome: Turn one tested workflow into a small reusable skill, then decide whether the job also needs a governed connection to external tools or data through MCP.

lessons.title: Write and test a skill
lessons.outcome: Package the durable method from your recurring job into a concise skill brief with clear triggers, degrees of freedom, safety boundaries and blind tests.
lessons.exercise: Choose one repeated part of your workflow that has succeeded at least twice, write its skill brief from real examples, then give its blind evaluation prompts to a fresh session or colleague without showing the expected answer and record every miss.

artifact.description: A reusable skill brief containing its trigger, non-trigger, inputs, ordered workflow, degree of freedom, resource map, safety boundaries, output contract and results from normal, ambiguous and out-of-scope blind tests.

verification: The skill brief starts from at least two real examples rather than from an imagined general-purpose capability.
Its trigger and non-trigger let a fresh reader decide when the skill should and should not be used.
Each fragile step has tighter instructions while judgement-heavy steps retain a stated degree of freedom.
The blind evaluation prompts do not reveal the expected answer or the failure the test is meant to expose.
A miss changed the instructions, resource map or boundary and the revised skill was tested again.

content.text: A skill is a reusable way of doing work

A skill packages the part of a workflow that should survive a conversation. It tells an AI system when a method applies, which inputs matter, what sequence to follow, where judgement is allowed, what must never happen and what a finished result looks like. It is more than a saved prompt because it carries the checks and the boundaries as well as the request.

Start from work you have already done. Two real examples reveal the decisions you make without noticing, the places where sources differ and the exceptions that a generic instruction misses. A skill invented before the workflow has run usually packages guesses. Run the job, record the repeated method, then package what survived.

The goal is not to preserve every sentence from the successful conversation. Keep what a capable system cannot safely rediscover each time: your policy, source hierarchy, required order, output contract, stopping rules and examples of the boundary. Leave facts in their source and point to them. Context has a cost, and a large skill can hide the rule that actually matters.
Choose the degree of freedom
Low freedom fits fragile exact work. Give the precise source, order, required fields and failure response. A calculation or approved filing template should not be improvised.
Medium freedom fits a known method with variable material. State the stages and checks, then allow the system to choose how to organise the evidence inside them.
High freedom fits exploratory work where several routes can be valid. Keep the evidence, privacy and authority boundaries explicit even when the route is open.

Do not choose one freedom level for the whole job. A research brief may allow broad exploration while requiring exact citation fields and a fixed refusal when evidence is missing. Tighten the step that fails dangerously, not every sentence around it.
Keep the core small and route the rest

The core instructions should let a reader understand the trigger, the workflow and the boundaries in one pass. Put long policy, examples and templates in named references. Use a script only for a narrow deterministic operation that is safer to run than to describe repeatedly. Use an asset only when the output needs a real template or approved visual material.

Every resource needs a reason. If the core never points to it, remove it. If it changes independently, give it an owner and update trigger. A forgotten reference is worse than no reference because it looks authoritative while quietly teaching an old rule.
Test the skill without leaking the answer

A blind evaluation prompt gives the task and permitted inputs without telling the worker which rule you hope it will apply. If the prompt says remember to refuse when the approval is missing, you tested obedience to the hint, not whether the skill made the boundary usable.

Use at least three classes. A normal case should complete. An ambiguous case should ask a useful question or state the assumption it needs. An out-of-scope case should stop or route elsewhere. Add one plausible wrong result from your earlier check-with-teeth.md and confirm the skill does not accept it merely because the prose looks finished.

Record the first run before editing. A miss may show an unclear instruction, missing example, unreachable resource, wrong trigger or a task the skill should never have accepted. Repair the owning part, then rerun the same class with a fresh example. Do not keep adding warnings around a bad abstraction.
What you will make

Create the skill brief in skill-brief.md with name, description, trigger, non-trigger, required inputs, ordered workflow, degrees of freedom, output contract, resource map, safety boundaries and three blind evaluation prompts. Add a small results table with expected behaviour, observed behaviour, miss and repair.
Try it on your work
Pick one repeated stage with two completed examples and mark the decisions that recur.
Write the trigger and non-trigger before the procedure so the boundary shapes the skill.
Give each step low, medium or high freedom and explain why a mistake there is cheap or costly.
Route only necessary references, scripts and assets, with an owner for anything durable.
Run the normal, ambiguous and out-of-scope prompts blind. Repair one real miss and rerun.
Check your work
A fresh reader can distinguish when the skill fires from a nearby task it must refuse.
The core contains no fact or procedure that belongs in a maintained source.
The out-of-scope test stops cleanly without producing a helpful-looking substitute.
The ambiguous test asks for the missing decision rather than selecting one silently.
The results table records a miss and a verified repair rather than only successful examples.

lessons.title: Separate skills from MCP connections
lessons.outcome: Decide whether your recurring job needs reusable instructions, a connection to external systems, both, or neither, with the smallest permission and action boundary that can do the work.
lessons.exercise: Map every missing capability in the recurring job to instruction, current data or external action, choose skill, MCP, both or neither for each gap, then test the choice using invented or read-only material and record the permission and failure boundary.

artifact.description: A decision record separating workflow instruction from external access or action, naming the chosen skill and MCP roles, data and tool permissions, approval gates, fallback behaviour and evidence from a harmless test.

verification: Each gap is classified as missing instruction, missing access, missing action, missing authority or a task that should stay manual.
No skill is described as granting access that only a configured and authorised connection can provide.
Every MCP tool or resource requested is tied to one step and uses the narrowest useful permission.
The test uses read-only or invented material and proves the refusal path before any write action is considered.
The record states what happens when the connection is unavailable, returns stale data or requests unexpected authority.

content.text: Instruction and connection solve different gaps

A skill tells the AI how to carry out a repeated workflow. It packages the method, decisions, source hierarchy, output contract and safety boundary. It cannot make a file, database, calendar or business system available if the product has no authorised connection to it.

MCP connects an AI application to external systems through a standard protocol. Model Context Protocol is an open standard through which a server can expose tools for actions, resources for context and prompts for reusable interaction templates. The host application decides what it supports and how the user sees and approves those capabilities.

A skill is instruction. MCP is a connection contract. They can work together and neither replaces the other. A meeting-prep skill can say how to build a decision brief. An MCP connection can make approved calendar events and documents available. The skill still needs a rule for missing context, and the connection still needs permissions.

As of 14 August 2026, MCP is supported across several AI applications, but support, setup and approval vary by product and organisation. This lesson teaches the decision boundary, not a setup sequence. Check the current client and approved server before relying on any connection.
Choose among four honest answers
Choose a skill when the material is already available but the method gets reinvented or explained repeatedly.
Choose MCP when the method is clear but the job needs current data or a specific external capability that the AI application cannot otherwise reach.
Choose both when a repeated method needs governed access. Keep the method in the skill and the access boundary in the connection and its permissions.
Choose neither when a checklist, lookup, formula or person-only decision can do the job more clearly, or when authority is absent.

Do not add a connection because it exists. Each tool or resource adds data exposure, possible action and another failure mode. Name the exact step it enables. If you cannot, leave it disconnected. Least permission starts by refusing capabilities the workflow does not need.
Tools, resources and prompts

A tool is a callable function, such as searching a system, creating a draft record or performing a calculation. A resource supplies contextual data, such as a file, record or schema. A prompt is a reusable interaction template exposed through the protocol. These are protocol primitives, not promises about correctness or authorisation.

A connection can expose more than the task should use. Record read, create, modify, send, delete and schedule separately. Prefer read-only access for evidence gathering. Put any external write behind a person who can see the target, payload and consequence. Treat names and descriptions from an untrusted server as untrusted input rather than instructions to expand scope.

The failure contract matters as much as the happy path. What happens if the server is unavailable, the resource is stale, the tool returns partial data or a requested action is outside authority? A safe workflow produces a bounded draft, asks a question or stops. It does not quietly swap in remembered information.
Test access without testing damage

Begin with discovery and a read-only case. Confirm which tools and resources the client actually exposes, which account they belong to, and whether the returned source is current. Use invented material where a real record would be sensitive. Then remove the connection and confirm the workflow reaches its written fallback.

Do not test a write by sending a real message, moving a live file or changing a record. Prepare the proposed action, inspect the exact target and payload, and stop before execution. The safe-action lesson later in the course adds the approval and post-action evidence needed for a real authorised change.
What you will make

Create skill-mcp-decision.md. For each workflow gap, record its type, the skill or MCP role if any, exact tools or resources, data class, permissions, approval gate, fallback and evidence from one harmless test.
Try it on your work
List every place the workflow lacks a method, current fact, external action or authority.
Choose skill, MCP, both or neither for each gap and give the smallest reason that supports it.
For every proposed connection, list tools and resources and cross out anything not needed for this job.
Run one read-only or invented case, then run it with the connection absent to test the fallback.
Record any action the workflow can prepare but must not execute without explicit approval.
Check your work
Instruction gaps and access gaps are in separate rows and have different repairs.
Every connected tool or resource enables a named workflow step and nothing is connected just in case.
The permission list distinguishes reading from creating, changing, sending, deleting and scheduling.
The disconnected run follows the written fallback instead of inventing current data.
No real external change was used merely to prove that a connection works.

sections.title: Research and write with evidence
sections.outcome: Build an evidence-backed argument before drafting, then use AI as an editorial partner to repair structure and prose without inventing facts, voice or experience.

lessons.title: Research before you draft
lessons.outcome: Define the decision, build a dated claim-status table, test the thesis and its strongest counterargument, and gather missing evidence before asking for prose.
lessons.exercise: Take the next brief or recommendation inside your recurring job, write the intended decision and source hierarchy, classify every material claim, verify primary sources, map the argument, and delay drafting until the weakest link and strongest counterargument are visible.

artifact.description: A research pack containing the decision, source hierarchy, dated claim-status table, source ledger, first idea map, thesis stress test, strongest counterargument, weakest link, missing evidence and honest insufficient-evidence route.

verification: Every material claim is marked observed, inferred, disproved or unknown and carries a current supporting source where one exists.
A citation is checked for support at the exact location rather than accepted because the source looks authoritative.
The strongest counterargument could change the recommendation and is not a softened version written to be dismissed.
The weakest link names the missing fact or reasoning step that would most affect the intended decision.
The pack has a not-enough-evidence route and no unknown claim has been turned into polished prose.

content.text: Name the decision before the topic

Research gets vague when the request is a topic. Research the market, understand the policy or look into the incident gives the system no test for relevance. Name the person who will read the work, the decision they face, the date or period that matters and the form of answer they can act on.

The decision narrows the evidence. A background fact may be interesting and still irrelevant. A small contradiction may matter more than a large pile of agreement if it changes the recommendation. Write the decision at the top of the pack and make every source earn its place against it.

Set a source hierarchy before searching. Current primary material comes first for product behaviour, policy, law, financial figures or official decisions. Internal records and prior cases are leads whose current status must be checked. Reviews and interviews show reported experience, not universal fact. Search results and generated summaries help you find a source and do not replace opening it.
Build the claim-status table
Observed means the source directly establishes the claim you wrote, for the relevant scope and date.
Inferred means the conclusion follows from evidence plus a reasoning step. Keep the step visible and invite challenge.
Disproved means current evidence contradicts the claim. Keep it in the table so it cannot return later as an unexamined assumption.
Unknown means the evidence is absent, conflicting, stale or outside your authority to obtain. Unknown is a result, not a drafting inconvenience.

For each row, record the claim, status, source, source date, date checked, exact supporting location and what would disprove it. Then do the fact-check at the source. A link proves where a statement came from. It does not prove that the source supports the wording, that the source is right, or that the claim is complete.

Ask the AI to help inspect the table, not bless it. Useful requests include finding claims with no source, comparing the wording with the cited passage, naming scope changes, and proposing what evidence would overturn the inference. Open the source yourself for any claim that changes the decision.
Map and stress-test the argument

Make an idea map before a draft. Put the intended takeaway at the top. Under it, place the few claims it needs. Under each claim, put the evidence and the reasoning step. Anything that does not support the takeaway becomes background, a separate question or material to cut.

Now ask for the strongest counterargument, not a polite objection. It should use the same evidence standard and state the condition under which it wins. If your reply is that the reader would never think that, you have probably not written the strongest version. Give it enough force that it could change the recommendation.

Name the weakest link next. It may be a stale source, a jump from correlation to cause, an untested assumption about the reader, or a policy interpretation that needs an authorised owner. Gather the missing material before polishing. If it cannot be obtained, narrow the claim or take the not enough evidence route.

This is an editorial partnership rather than a request for an answer. You provide the decision, source boundary and accountability. The AI helps expose omissions, contradictions and rival structures. You decide which claims survive and whether the evidence is strong enough to adopt them.
What you will make

Create research-evidence-pack.md with the decision, reader, source hierarchy, claim-status table, source ledger, idea map, thesis, strongest counterargument, weakest link, missing-evidence list and the explicit route for not enough evidence.
Try it on your work
Write the reader, decision and relevant date before opening a search tool.
List the claims the decision would need and give each a status before drafting.
Open every consequential source, capture the exact support and mark scope or date limits.
Draw the idea map, then ask for the strongest counterargument and weakest link.
Gather the missing evidence or narrow the claim. Only then start the draft.
Check your work
The decision and reader exclude at least one interesting but irrelevant source.
Every observed claim has exact support and every inference exposes its reasoning step.
The counterargument could win under a named condition and is not a token paragraph.
At least one claim was narrowed, removed or left unknown after checking the evidence.
No prose presents a citation as proof beyond the scope and date of the source.

lessons.title: Edit the argument and repair the prose
lessons.outcome: Revise the argument before line editing, preserve every supported claim and the accountable author's voice, and remove AI-writing patterns without inventing specificity.
lessons.exercise: Take a draft built from the research pack, compare its first and revised idea maps, resolve the strongest counterargument and weakest link, then run a voice-calibrated AI-writing repair and record every suggestion rejected for fabrication, tone or claim drift.

artifact.description: An editorial record containing the first and revised idea maps, claim-status changes, structural decisions, voice sample, pattern audit, fabrication check, rejected suggestions, final draft and cold-read notes.

verification: The revised idea map shows a material structural decision made before sentence-level changes began.
Every supported claim from the approved research pack remains supported after the rewrite or is explicitly removed.
The fabrication check rejects any invented quote, experience, number, motive, feeling or decorative specificity.
The prose is calibrated against a real sample from the accountable author rather than a generic instruction to sound human.
A cold read catches at least one unclear transition, repeated point or claim that still outruns its evidence.

content.text: Edit in the order the risk appears

A clean sentence cannot rescue a weak argument. Before asking for smoother prose, restate the intended takeaway, reopen the claim-status table and compare the draft with the idea map. Check whether the draft answers the decision, whether the evidence carries the thesis and whether the strongest counterargument received a real answer.

Structural editing comes first because it can remove, combine or reorder whole sections. A line edit performed before that work creates attachment to sentences you should cut. It also makes unsupported reasoning look finished, which is the most dangerous form of polish in professional writing.

Use AI as an editorial partner. Ask it to rebuild the idea map from the draft, identify the weakest link, name the paragraph where movement stops, and argue the strongest alternative structure. Do not ask whether the draft is good. Ask questions that produce evidence you can inspect.
Rebuild the map after revision

Make the structural changes, then rebuild the map from the revised draft without looking at the first map. The new map should show the actual argument, not the argument you remember intending. Compare them. A missing claim may be a useful cut or a broken link. A new claim may be a clearer inference or an unsupported addition.

Run the fact-check again after structural work. Moving a qualifier can widen a claim. Combining paragraphs can detach a source from the sentence it supported. Summarising can turn several bounded observations into a universal statement. Source validity did not change, but claim shape did.

Now cut repetition and audit the opening. The opening should earn the reader's attention with the real decision or tension, not a generic statement that the topic matters. Keep necessary context, but move it to the point where the reader needs it. End each section with a consequence, decision or next action rather than a summary of itself.
Repair AI writing without fabricating humanity

AI-writing repair is not synonym replacement and it is not an attempt to fool a detector. Preserve the supported information while changing the shape that makes the draft feel generic: repeated setup-conclusion pairs, equal-length paragraphs, over-explained transitions, padded lists, abstract claims and the assistant's habit of announcing what it will say.

Calibrate against a real sample from the person who will own the document. Notice sentence length, directness, preferred terms, tolerance for fragments, how claims are qualified and what the writer leaves implicit. Preserve deliberate roughness if it carries voice. Neutral prose may be the right voice for a legal note, policy or reference document.

Do not make a vague sentence vivid by inventing a number, anecdote or emotion. Do not add a quote nobody said or a motive the evidence does not establish. A fabrication check should inspect every new specific detail and ask where it came from. If the answer is that it merely sounds plausible, remove it.

Audit clusters rather than punctuation in isolation. One colon, one short sentence or one balanced phrase proves nothing. Repeated structure across the whole document is the signal. Read paragraphs in sequence and mark where the prose starts sounding interchangeable with any professional memo on any subject.
Keep a rejection record

An editorial partner should propose changes you reject. Record the significant ones. Rejection reasons reveal the writing contract: unsupported claim, invented detail, lost nuance, wrong audience, voice drift, unnecessary polish or a valid rough edge. The record is also evidence that you reviewed rather than adopted the rewrite whole.

Finish with a cold read after a break or by a second person. Read for movement, support and voice separately. The document can pass one and fail another. Update the claim table for any late cut or qualification, then name the accountable author who adopts the final text.
What you will make

Create editorial-repair-record.md with the first and revised maps, structural decisions, changed claim statuses, a short voice sample, pattern audit, fabrication check, rejected suggestions, cold-read notes and a pointer to the final draft.
Try it on your work
Rebuild the first idea map from the draft and compare it with the intended takeaway.
Resolve the weakest link and strongest counterargument before touching sentence style.
Revise structure, rebuild the map and rerun the fact-check against the new claim shapes.
Run the voice and pattern audit, then apply only the repairs that preserve support and intent.
Complete the fabrication check, record rejected suggestions and perform a cold read.
Check your work
The revised map makes the decision path easier to inspect and no required claim disappeared silently.
The final claim table matches the actual wording and qualifiers in the final draft.
Every new specific detail has a source and no human texture was invented for effect.
The rejection record includes at least one plausible suggestion that would have weakened truth or voice.
The cold read produced a concrete correction rather than a general feeling that the draft sounded fine.

sections.title: Produce work and act safely
sections.outcome: Build and inspect professional documents, spreadsheets and meeting briefs, then keep every external action behind explicit authority and post-action evidence.

lessons.title: Build and check work artefacts
lessons.outcome: Create the document, spreadsheet or meeting brief your recurring job needs and prove its source, content, calculation and rendered-output checks separately.
lessons.exercise: Choose the professional artefact your recurring job actually delivers, build it from the approved evidence pack, inspect both its underlying content and rendered form, then run one deliberately broken source, calculation or decision case through the relevant check.

artifact.description: A quality record naming the artefact, reader and decision, with source and content checks plus the relevant document render, spreadsheet reconciliation or meeting-preparation checks and evidence from one deliberate failure.

verification: The chosen format follows the reader's decision and information shape rather than the easiest generation tool.
Source and content checks are recorded separately from layout, calculation and rendered-output checks.
A document was inspected page by page, a spreadsheet reconciled and rendered, or a meeting brief checked against its event and sources.
One plausible broken input or calculation caused a named check to fail before the artefact was accepted.
The final quality record states what remains unverified and who must review it before professional use.

content.text: Choose the form from the work

A professional artefact is not finished when the text exists. It has a reader, a decision or action, a source boundary, a form and a quality gate. Choose the form from what the reader needs to inspect. Use prose for an argument, steps for a procedure, a table for repeated comparable records and a spreadsheet when calculations and assumptions need to remain visible.

Keep factual correctness, structural usefulness, calculation, visual quality, privacy and accessibility as separate checks. A polished document can carry a false claim. A correct spreadsheet can hide a broken formula. A complete meeting summary can still omit the decision the meeting exists to make.

Begin from the work contract and research evidence pack. Name the reader and next action, then map each information unit to the form that makes it inspectable. Do not ask for a beautiful file before the source and content contract is settled. Visual polish is a later proof, not a substitute for the first ones.
Document lane

For a document, choose its mode: decision memo, proposal, procedure, report or brief. Lead with the decision, next action or result the reader came for. Use headings to expose the argument, tables only for repeated comparable facts, and callouts for a boundary the reader could otherwise miss.

Render the document to pages and inspect every page. Check clipping, broken tables, orphan headings, unreadable footnotes, inconsistent spacing, source placement and whether the visual hierarchy matches the intellectual hierarchy. Text extraction cannot prove layout. A polished page cannot prove factual support. Record both gates.

When editing an existing file, preserve its structure and metadata unless the task says otherwise. Comments, tracked changes and hidden fields can carry private material that a page image does not reveal. Review them separately before sharing.
Spreadsheet lane

For a spreadsheet, separate inputs, assumptions, calculations and outputs. Keep source dates and units beside inputs. Use simple formulas for derived values instead of hard-coded totals or magic numbers. A reader should be able to trace an output to the exact cells and assumptions that produced it.

Test zero, negative, missing and duplicated inputs where they make sense. Scan for formula errors, reconcile representative totals against the source and inspect whether copied formulas point at the intended rows. Then render every sheet and check widths, number formats, hidden columns, page breaks, chart labels and whether displayed precision matches meaning.

A nearby label does not prove that a formula uses the labelled assumption. Open the formula and trace it. A total that matches once can still be wrong through two cancelling errors, so reconcile components as well as the grand total.
Meeting lane

For a meeting brief, start with the event and inspect its linked material. Infer the likely decision carefully and label the inference. Separate confirmed context from missing context. Prioritise what somebody must read, decide or prepare rather than copying the calendar description into a longer summary.

A useful brief names the purpose, likely decisions, confirmed facts, missing inputs, questions, owners and pre-meeting actions. It does not invent an agenda from a thin invitation. If the purpose remains uncertain, the first useful action is a question to the organiser.
Clearly illustrative accountant exercise

This is invented teaching material, not accounting advice or a real organisation. An accountant prepares a month-end variance workpaper from approved current and prior-period reports. The workbook keeps raw inputs separate, records the reporting period and currency, reconciles source totals, calculates variances with formulas, flags unmatched accounts and leaves journal entries outside the permitted action boundary.

The acceptance check is not that the commentary sounds plausible. It requires source totals to reconcile, every material narrative to point to a row, missing accounts to remain visible and a qualified reviewer to approve the workpaper. Break the case by duplicating one source row. The reconciliation must fail before the narrative is accepted.
What you will make
