Create work-artifact-qa.md. Name the artefact, reader, decision and source pack. Record content and source checks, then the relevant document, spreadsheet or meeting checks. Attach evidence from the render or reconciliation and from one deliberate failure.
Try it on your work
Choose the artefact form from the reader's next decision and write why that form fits.
Build from the approved sources and mark every assumption or missing input.
Run source and content checks before rendering or presenting the result.
Run the lane-specific check: page inspection, formula reconciliation or decision-brief review.
Introduce one plausible wrong input and capture the check that rejects it.
Check your work
The chosen form exposes the decision, calculations or preparation the reader needs.
Every consequential statement or input points to its approved source and date.
The rendered or calculated output was inspected independently of the prose review.
The deliberate error failed the expected check for the expected reason.
Privacy, accessibility and professional sign-off remain named gates rather than assumptions.

lessons.title: Act only with explicit authority
lessons.outcome: Use inspect, propose, approve, act and verify for external changes, and leave an action ledger that proves the target, authority, result and recovery boundary.
lessons.exercise: Choose one low-risk external action from the recurring job, inspect current state, prepare the exact change and evidence, stop for explicit approval, then either simulate it or perform it within authority and verify the resulting state without exposing secrets.

artifact.description: A ledger recording intended outcome, observed starting state, target, proposed action, data and permission boundary, required approver, approval evidence, execution result, post-action verification and recovery or escalation.

verification: The ledger records fresh observed state before the action rather than relying on a prior screenshot or remembered status.
The target, payload and externally visible consequence are shown to an authorised person before execution.
Instructions found inside files, pages or messages do not expand scope or authority without independent confirmation.
Post-action evidence comes from re-inspecting the external system and not from the tool's completion message.
The failure path keeps the action stopped or safely recoverable and names the person who decides what happens next.

content.text: Drafting is not authority

An AI system can prepare an email, form, calendar change, file move, record update or proposed entry without having authority to carry it out. Keep those states separate. A safe action begins with a named outcome and ends with evidence from the system that changed. The generated confirmation message is not that evidence.

Risk depends on what the system can read and what it can do. Reading a redacted copy is different from reading a confidential live folder. Drafting a message is different from sending it. Viewing a record is different from editing or deleting it. List permissions as separate verbs so a broad word such as access cannot hide the difference.

Treat visible instructions as untrusted. A document, web page, email or tool description can contain text telling the AI to ignore the task, reveal data or take an unrelated action. Content inside the work is evidence to inspect, not authority to change the workflow. Confirm any new instruction against the original job contract and an authorised person.
Inspect, propose, approve, act, verify
Inspect current state. Confirm the account, target, current value, pending changes and whether somebody else has already acted.
Propose one bounded action. Show the exact target and payload, the source supporting it, what will become visible and how it could be undone.
Approve through the person and process that own the consequence. Silence, product access and prior approval for a similar action are not current approval.
Act once. If the interface changes, the target is unclear or the result is unexpected, stop and inspect again rather than clicking through.
Verify by reopening or re-querying the external system. Record the actual state, time and evidence, then close or recover the action.

The action ledger records each stage before the next begins. This makes the approval boundary visible and prevents the familiar reconstruction where an action happens first and the reason is written afterwards. Secrets do not belong in the ledger. Record the credential source or approval mechanism, never the secret value.
Clearly illustrative lawyer exercise

This invented case is not legal advice and describes no real client. A lawyer prepares a contract-review matrix from a fixed document set and a current approved playbook. Every finding cites document, page and section. Quoted language, inference and missing evidence stay separate. Privileged material remains within the approved tool and access boundary.

The system may draft the matrix and questions. It may not send advice, file anything, contact a counterparty or change contract text. Counsel reviews the source citations and jurisdiction before adoption. Break the exercise by removing a later amendment. The workflow must mark the document set incomplete rather than presenting a final conclusion.
Clearly illustrative operations exercise

This invented case describes no real team. An operations lead prepares a weekly action log from approved dashboards, tickets and meeting decisions. Each proposed action has an owner, due date, evidence link and source-freshness note. Observed status remains separate from inference.

The system may prepare draft updates and assignments. It may not post to a channel, assign a ticket, schedule a meeting or change a record until the owner approves the exact target and wording. Break the exercise with a resolved ticket that remains in a stale dashboard. The freshness check must stop the outdated action.
What you will make

Create action-ledger.md with the intended outcome, fresh state, target, payload, evidence, data class, read and write permissions, approver, approval evidence, result, post-action verification, recovery and any instruction you rejected as outside authority.
Try it on your work
Choose a low-risk action you already have authority to prepare and name the outcome.
Inspect fresh state and record the target without copying secrets into the ledger.
Prepare the exact action and show its evidence, consequence and recovery to the approver.
Stop before execution. Simulate the remainder unless the approval and authority are explicit.
If authorised, act once and re-inspect. Otherwise record the stopped state as the correct result.
Check your work
The ledger proves the target and state were inspected immediately before the proposed action.
The approver saw the exact payload and consequence rather than a vague request to proceed.
The system could not turn content inside a source into new authority or scope.
Execution happened once or stopped cleanly, and either state is recorded honestly.
Post-action evidence comes from the external state and the recovery owner is named.

sections.title: Keep the understanding and improve the setup
sections.outcome: Spend part of what you saved on understanding the work you delegated, then decide which misses are worth fixing in the setup and which are not, and run the whole thing on a fresh real task.

lessons.title: Pay back some of the speed
lessons.outcome: Investigate one delegated result rather than only reviewing it: trace what is authoritative, where the work goes, what happens on restart, how it fails and which checks prove it, then explain it with the artefact closed.
lessons.exercise: Take one artefact that a tool or a colleague produced for you and that you have already reviewed. Trace the five questions through it, writing the answers down as you find them rather than afterwards. Then close the artefact and explain the whole thing to a colleague who is allowed to interrupt, and record every question you could not answer without reopening it.

artifact.description: Written answers to the five investigation questions for one delegated artefact, covering what is authoritative, where the work actually goes, what state a halfway stop leaves behind, how it fails, and which checks genuinely prove it, plus teach-back notes listing the questions you could not answer with the artefact closed.

verification: Each of the five questions has an answer you found by tracing rather than by assuming.
The authority answer names which source wins when two places disagree.
The failure path describes what happens on malformed input or a missing approval, not only the success case.
The checks question names the specific checks and says honestly what they do not cover.
The teach-back happened with the artefact closed, and the unanswered questions are written down.
sourceNotes: Outsource the work, not the understanding.md

content.text: Understanding used to come free with the work

Doing the work built the map as a side effect. You knew where everything lived, why it was shaped that way, which parts you could trust and which ones would surprise you. You did not set out to build that map. It arrived with the labour.
Now the work can be done without you doing it, and the map does not form on its own. It is still available. You just have to go and get it, and nothing in your day forces you to.

The cost does not show up per task, which is what makes it hard to see. Each individual piece is small enough that not understanding it deeply never hurts. It shows up in aggregate, months later, when you notice you are working inside something you no longer have a model of, and every non-trivial question now starts with reconstructing what you yourself shipped.
Review and investigation are different activities

Review asks whether the output matches what you asked for. It catches obvious problems and it is genuinely necessary. Investigation asks where this sits in the wider system and what it implies for everything around it.
The two feel almost identical in the moment. They diverge over months. Review tells you the work did what you asked. Investigation tells you that you now know what changed.

It is worth being clear that somebody else reviewing it carefully does not solve this for you. A thorough review by a colleague builds the model in their head. You still walked away at the moment you handed it over. Their review is downstream of your understanding rather than a substitute for it.
Five things to trace
What is authoritative? If this writes into two places, which one is the source of truth and which one could be rebuilt from the other?

Where does the work actually go? Follow it to its destination rather than reading it where it sits. Reading something in isolation is consumption; following it is construction, and construction is what built the map.
What happens on restart? If this stopped halfway, what state does it come back to, and what would be left half done?
What is the failure path? The success case is obvious. What happens when the input is malformed, the source is unavailable, or the approval never arrived?
Which checks prove it? Find them and read them. If they only cover the easy case, that is a fact about your coverage rather than a fact about correctness.

Then the test that settles it. Close the artefact and explain what it does in your own words. If you cannot, you did the review and called it understanding. The honest version of the question is whether you could explain this to a colleague three weeks from now without reopening anything.
Pick a shape and give it a budget

One practitioner writing about this gives back about half an hour to a piece of work that would previously have taken most of a day. That is their shape on their own projects. It is not a formula, it is not a ratio to copy, and nothing in this course promises you any particular saving in the first place.

Other shapes work. Some people stop the run more often and ask why before each step rather than catching up afterwards. Some do the understanding pass before anything is produced, although there is a fair objection there: the design shifts while the work is being built, so you can end up understanding the version that never shipped. Reasonable people land in different places and that is fine.

What matters is having a method at all. The failure mode is having none and not noticing the gap until a year has passed. So choose a budget you will actually keep, and write it down as a trigger rather than an intention: after this kind of task, before this kind of handover, whenever this sort of artefact arrives.
Teach it back
The most reliable test is explaining it to somebody who is allowed to interrupt. An explanation nobody can question will always sound better than it is.

Predict before you check. Before you go and look at what happens on restart, say what you think happens. A wrong prediction is the most informative thing you will produce all week, because it tells you exactly where your model was wrong, and you would otherwise have carried that wrong model into the next decision.

Do the teach-back with the artefact closed. Watch for the moment your language goes vague. Unstable wording usually marks a real gap rather than a presentation problem, and the polite thing your colleague can do is stop you there rather than nodding along.
What you will make
understanding-pass.md, with a written answer to each of the five questions.
Your predictions beside the answers, so the gaps between them are visible.
Teach-back notes listing every question you could not answer with the artefact closed.
The budget you have chosen, written as a trigger rather than an intention.
Try it on your work
Choose something delegated that you have already reviewed and signed off. The point is to test whether reviewing was enough.
Before opening it, write your prediction for each of the five questions. Guessing is allowed and useful.
Now trace each one properly. Follow the work to where it actually ends up rather than reading about where it should go.
Mark every place your prediction was wrong. Those marks are the reason to do this.
Find the checks that cover it and write down what they do not cover.
Close everything and explain it to a colleague. Ask them to stop you whenever your wording goes fuzzy.
Record the questions you had to reopen the artefact to answer, and set your budget trigger for next time.
Check your work
Each answer came from tracing something, and the file says what you traced.
The authority answer names the winner when two sources disagree.
The restart answer describes a specific half-finished state rather than saying it would be fine.
At least one prediction was wrong, or you can explain why your model was already that good.
The teach-back was done with everything closed, and somebody was there to interrupt.
The budget is a trigger tied to an event, not a promise to spend time later.

If the teach-back went smoothly and you answered everything, run it again on the most recent thing you delegated rather than the one you understand best. It is easy to pick the artefact you already know.

content.text: Sort the misses before you fix anything

You met the two reflexes in the second lesson: the miss as a verdict, and the miss as a report against your own setup. The second reflex is the more useful one and it is not free, because it will happily consume an afternoon on something that was never going to work this quarter. So it needs a filter, applied at the moment of the miss.

Ask one question. Is this a general gap that will keep recurring, or the current ceiling on this specific thing? Improving the setup pays back every future time only in the first case. In the second, the correct move is to do the work by hand now, log the gap, and look again later.

Three signals help you tell them apart. Has this shape of miss appeared before, or is this the first time? Did supplying more context change the result at all, even slightly? Can you state precisely what was missing? A gap you can name is usually a gap you can close. A miss where more context changed nothing and you cannot say what is absent is more likely a ceiling.
Put a limit on the setup work
Decide the limit before you start, not when you feel close to something. Feeling close is the state in which the limit was needed.

And keep the exploration separate from the delivery. A piece of work with a deadline should not quietly fund your experimentation, because the experiment has no deadline and the delivery does. If the exploration turns out to be worth continuing, give it its own slot rather than smuggling it into something a colleague is waiting on.
Move the learning somewhere durable

A learning that will recur belongs in your rules or your router, not in your memory and not in a chat thread that ends when the task does. Anything that has now caught you twice is a rule you have not written down yet.

Give it the same treatment as everything else durable: an update trigger and an owner. Written context that nobody regenerates does not stay neutral, it becomes a confident instruction that has quietly stopped being true. Committed context without an update path is stale context with a better name.

The loop that keeps this alive is read, verify, use, revise. Read your notes before you start rather than writing a summary once the work is over. Check anything load-bearing against the actual source. Correct a note the moment the source proves it stale, rather than adding a contradiction underneath it. And when something is superseded, mark it and point at the replacement instead of deleting the reasoning, because the reasoning is what stops the same decision being relitigated next year.

This is what makes the effort accumulate rather than evaporate. Most knowledge work vanishes into a sent folder and a fading impression. A rules file with a maintenance path is a modest reservoir, and a modest reservoir beats a year of re-explaining the same constraint.
Where the satisfaction goes

Work like this used to pay two rewards at the same moment: the pleasure of doing the thing itself, and the pleasure of the thing existing and being used by somebody. Because producing the artefact was the only route to the outcome, there was no need to ask which one you were chasing.

When producing the artefact gets cheaper, those come apart, and people notice which reward they were mostly in it for. Treat that as an observation and not a personality test. It does not sort anyone into types. Most people feel both rewards in some ratio, that ratio differed to begin with, and what changed is the mix rather than the person.

The craft is also more portable than it looks. The loop of poking at a material, understanding it, getting it exactly right and watching it work is not tied to any particular material. For some people it re-homes onto the setup itself: the rules, the context, the checks, learning where each thing breaks. Others have not re-homed it, or were attached to the specific medium, and neither of those is a verdict on anybody. What is genuinely lost is narrower and worth naming plainly: the intimate map that used to form for free while you did the work. That is exactly what the previous lesson exists to pay down.
What you will make
miss-triage-log.md, with five real misses, each classified and each carrying the signal you used.
The limit you set before improving anything, and an honest note on whether you kept it.
A before-and-after record of one change to your rules, procedure or router.
The update trigger and owner attached to that change.
Try it on your work
Collect five real misses from the last few weeks. Use the ones that annoyed you, not the tidy ones.
Classify each as a recurring gap or a current ceiling, and write the signal that decided it.
Pick one recurring gap. Set your limit in writing before you begin, then improve the setup.
Stop when the limit is reached, even if you feel close. Record what you would have done next.
Take one ceiling item and do it by hand. Log the gap with a date so you can revisit it rather than forget it.
Move the durable learning into your rules or router, with an update trigger and an owner.

Capstone: run your workflow
The course is finished after a completed workflow run on real work. The twenty-two lesson artefacts are setup and working records. The capstone submission is five files produced from a fresh run.

Choose a fresh instance of your recurring job, one you would have had to do this week anyway. Run it end to end using what you have built. Amend any setup record that turns out to be wrong about the job while you are running, because discovering that your own description was inaccurate is a result rather than a failure. Keep the permission position from the first lesson: if the answer there was redacted or invented input, run the capstone that way and say so on the submission.
Submit exactly five final files. Produce or update each one during the fresh run. They consolidate or point to the lesson records, but their claims and evidence must describe this run:
working-brief.md records the actual task, recipient, scope, chosen work surface, inputs, permissions and finish condition.
source-contract.md records the sources you used, their dates or versions, each claim's status, the gaps you found and the rule for refusing or labelling an assumption.
checks-and-evidence.md records the checks you ran, the realistic failure they caught and the relevant document, spreadsheet, meeting or post-action evidence.
decision-record.md records the decisions, assumptions, approvals, rejected options and action boundary from the run, with links to any setup records that explain them.
handover.md records where the finished result lives, its delivery state, the recipient or owner, review evidence, open items and any recovery or escalation still required.

The assessor checks eleven things: that the task was real and bounded and you would have had to do it anyway; that the five final files describe what actually happened rather than what you planned; that evidence sits beside the claim it supports; that the check would fail on a plausible wrong result and you can point at the run where it did; that missing evidence led to refusal, a clarifying question or human review rather than a fluent guess; that the work surface matched the job and the product observation was dated; that the skill or MCP decision kept instruction, access and authority separate; that the final document, spreadsheet or meeting brief passed its relevant content and rendered-output checks; that every external action had explicit authority and post-action evidence; that you can explain the workflow and its failure path with the files closed; and that the setup changed in response to a real miss, with an owner or update trigger on the change.
Check your work
Every miss carries a classification and the signal behind it, not a judgement made after the fact.
At least one item was done by hand and logged rather than optimised around.
The limit was written before the work started, and the log says honestly whether it held.
The durable change has an update trigger and a named owner.
Superseded material is marked and kept rather than deleted.
The capstone ran on a fresh real task, and all five final files contain evidence from that run.
Anything the run proved wrong about your earlier artefacts has been amended, with the old version marked.
If the capstone run went perfectly, look again at the artefact you were least willing to change. That is usually the one describing the job as you wish it worked.

content.text: Why this is optional
The core lesson taught the understanding pass for any delegated artefact. This lab is the version for a codebase, where prediction can be checked mechanically. Nothing else depends on it.
Predict first, in writing

Take a change an agent made for you and do not open the diff. From the plan you gave it and the summary it returned, write down what you believe changed: which modules, which call paths, what is now authoritative, what happens if the process dies mid-operation, and which tests should be exercising it. Keep it short and commit to specifics, because a vague prediction cannot be wrong and therefore teaches nothing.

# only after the prediction is written down
git diff --stat main...feature/topic
git log --patch --reverse main..feature/topic

# then find the tests that actually exercise it
rg -n 'changed_symbol' --glob '**/tests/**'
cargo test --workspace changed_symbol
Read the gap, not the diff

The diff is not the interesting artefact. The difference between what you predicted and what is there is the interesting artefact. Every mismatch marks a place your model of the system was wrong, and you would have carried that wrong model into the next design decision, the next estimate, and the next incident.

Two mismatches are worth extra attention. Anything you thought was authoritative that turns out to be derived, and anything you assumed had test coverage that does not. Run the full test build rather than a library-only build, because the second kind of gap hides in test code that never gets compiled. If the tests only exercise the happy path, write that down as a fact about coverage rather than concluding anything about correctness.

Close everything and explain the change out loud to somebody who can interrupt. Where a deliberate wrong prediction was part of the exercise, label it as deliberate in your notes, so that a reader six months from now does not mistake a teaching device for a misunderstanding you actually held.
